Closed-Head, Focal Lesions for Study of Repair in Immature Rat Cerebral Cortex. 
DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOBIOLOGY, 3(4): 21 7-223. Multiple electrocon- 
vulsive shocks consistently and rapidly produce uniform, bilaterally symmetrical 
lesions in the immature rat’s cerebral cortex, without the incidental damage that 
accompanies other experimental injuries to the central nervous system. The ter- 
minal lesion, devoid of nerve cells, is a narrow, laminar band of numerous myel- 
inated axons, unaccompanied by a glial scar. Insofar as the initially damaged area 
becomes occupied by nerve fibers, the healing process may be thought of as 
involving a regeneration. A variety of studies for which the electroshock lesions 
might be used is suggested.

Repeated application of electric current to the infant rat’s head by means of 
externally placed electrodes produces small, bilateral, symmetrical lesions pri- 
marily in layers iv and v of the cerebral cortex (Fig. 1A and B), useful for the 
study of healing processes in immature neural tissue. This method of making a 
lesion avoids immediate damage to the blood vessels and leptomeninges, gross 
hemorrhage, and total tissue necrosis, which complicate the study of wound 
repair in the central nervous system after injury produced by other means (e.g., 
excision, laceration, puncture, freezing, and ultrasonic, laser beam, or high-dose 
ionizing radiation). Additional advantages of the method are the simplicity of 
the procedure and of the apparatus required, the almost 100% survival rate after 
treatment (although a death may occasionally occur over the next few days), 
and the avoidance of surgical incision of the scalp and skull. Indeed, so far as we 
know, no other method of equal simplicity exists for the production of similar 
lesions. Much the same type of laminar cortical lesion has, however, been pro- 
duced in older animals with a beam of heavy ionizing particles, but this requires 
the use of a cyclotron or linear accelerator (Estable-Puig, de Estable, Tobias, & 
Haymaker, 1964; Janssen, Klatzo, Miquel, Brustad, Behar, Haymaker, Lyman, 
Henry, &Tobias, 1962; Kruger & Clemente, 1964; Malis, Baker, Kruger, &Rose, 
1957; Malis, Loevinger, Kruger, & Rose, 1957; Maxwell & Kruger, 1964; Rose, 
Malis, Kruger, & Baker, 1960). 
The electrodes used in our procedure are made from silver wire, balled at 
one end (diameter, 2.5-3mm), and coiled to make them slightly springy. The 
balled end is wrapped in layers of cotton-filled gauze sponge, tied down with 
surgical silk thread, and neatly trimmed beyond the tie, to yield a fairly soft or 
spongy, rounded surface. The free end of each electrode is mounted in a pair of 
plastic pliers so that the interelectrode distance can be easily adjusted for differ- 
ences in skull size among infant rats. Leads soldered to the mounted electrodes 
are plugged into a 60 cycle AC constant voltage stimulator, made simply from a 
Variac (0-120 V range) connected in series with a voltage regulating transformer. 
In series with the stimulator is an electronic timer (General Electric, model no. 
CR7504-A142), calibrated in 0.05 sec steps, with a timing range of 0 to 1.05 sec. 
The timer, operated by a foot switch, permits current to flow from the stimu- 
lator to the electrodes for a preset interval only. 
Before use, the electrodes are dipped in physiological saline which, for our 
purpose, provides a considerably better, less irritating medium for electrode-skin 
contact than electrode paste. While the electrodes and their site of placement 
should be well moistened with saline, care should be taken to avoid wetting 
neighboring s h n areas lest extraneous current paths be established. With the 
animal lightly held on a wooden table by the experimenter’s thumb and fore- 
finger, the electrodes are firmly applied to either side of the head, just medial 
and rostra1 to the base of the ear buds, and the current is turned on for 0.3 sec. 
The voltage used is 85 V. The animal responds to the electrostimulation with a

tonic convulsion characterized by body rigidity; severe tonic flexion of the rear 
limbs and often forward extension of the front limbs, the latter sometimes 
displaying delicate fluttering activity; downward movement of the forelimbs so 
that they extend rigidly below and toward the rear of the animal; rising, outward 
arching of the back and expansion of the chest, often a brief cessation of 
respiration with accompanying cyanosis; and digging and/or fluttering move- 
ments of the limbs, Thirty shocks are administered in a 34 min interval. This 
period provides ample time for relaxation from the rigidity induced by the 
preceding shock and, in most cases, for return of the animal’s color. It is also 
long enough for as many as 8 rats, even more with experience, to be treated, one 
after the other, before the turn of the first-shocked rat occurs again. During the 
90-120 min required for the entire procedure the litter is kept away from the 
mother and warmed under a 60-watt bulb. Control animals from each litter are 
subjected to the same manipulations, i.e., 30 applications of electrodes to the 
head, at a 3-4 min interval, but without the electrostimulation. 
The lesion-producing factors used (0.3 sec stimulation, 85 V, 30 shocks, 3 
to 4 min interval between shocks) were chosen after the effects of many differ- 
ent combinations had been studied. The factors selected regularly lead to the 
rapid development of a uniform series of pathological changes in the cerebral 
cortex. In good part the minimal damage produced in the scalp, and the remark- 
ably small loss of animals, can also be attributed to the factors used. (Some of 
our results suggest, however, that 30 shocks may be excessive; quite likely the 
minimal number required to produce a lesion, keeping the other factors con- 
stant, is between 20 and 30.) The lesions are located in the line of, and subjacent 
to, the site of electrode placement. Presumably they are mainly the result of 
electrically generated heat, as are small foci of injury in the skin at the electrode 
sites. Other factors involved in the passage of an alternating current through 
brain tissue, e.g., ionic and molecular oscillations (Zeman, 1968), may con- 
tribute to the damage, as may additional, though poorly defined, so-called 
specific electric effects. The latter, Zeman (1968) indicates, have been invoked 
by some workers to account for histopathological changes induced in the brain 
by currents supposedly too weak to have yielded significant thermal effects. 
In our study of the reaction of the developing cerebral cortex to injury, 
Columbia-Sherman rats (Rattus nowegicus), 4 to 4 1/2 days old when treated, 
were killed immediately at the end of the 30 shocks, at 3-hr intervals for the 
next 24 hr, then at 36 and 48 hr, thereafter daily for the next 5 days, then at a 1 
to 7 day interval for the following 9 weeks, and later at more widely spaced 
periods until 19 months of age. Histological examination of the brains revealed 
no lesions in the control animals. The severe seizures associated with the shocks 
did not lead to any apparent neuropathological changes such as might have been 
anticipated as a result of repeated short episodes of hypoxia. Briefly, the devel- 
opment and resolution of the lesions included the rapid occurrence of a localized

focus of edema and a loss of nerve cells, a short period of phagocytosis, a 
proliferation of myelin-forming glial cells, and the appearance of an abundance 
of myelinated axons in the damaged area. A detailed account of the pathological 
changes and a discussion of the histopathogenesis of these lesions has recently 
been published (Cowen, Geller, & Wolf, 1970). The lesion in its final form was a 
clearly demarcated, narrow, laminar band of myelinated fibers exceeding in 
number that of the normal cortex (Fig. 1A and B). It was free of glial scarring. 
Superficial to the lesion myelination of the cortex was often deficient. Although 
the final, laminar lesion did not contain nerve cell bodies, the deeper portion of 
the original, considerably larger, zone of injury had been repopulated by them, 
but their origin, at this point, is unclear. 
The occupation of the damaged area by axons, which became myelinated, 
may be thought of as constituting a regeneration. Whether this resulted from a 
regrowth of fibers from the proximal segments of initially injured axons, or from 
the entry into the lesion of fibers normally growing in the cortex during its 
active development, or perhaps from both, has yet to be determined. We believe 
that with appropriate techniques (electron microscopy, autoradiography , histo- 
chemistry) the electroshock lesions can be profitably employed for the study of 
such questions, as well as of other interesting and important topics, for example, 
differentiation of glial and nerve cell precursors and of glial cells per se, develop- 
ment of axons and of myelin sheaths, formation of abnormal glia, cell migration, 
and the regenerative capacity of nerve cells, in an area of focal injury in the 
immature central nervous system. Although we have not yet attempted to pro- 
duce electroshock lesions in older animals, it would be interesting to learn if 
such injuries would heal, as in the infant rats, with the formation of a band of 
myelinated fibers rather than a glial scar. 
Beyond their possible employment in the studies mentioned above, these 
simply produced, small, cortical lesions may also serve as useful models for the 
study of alterations in function after minimal brain damage sustained in infancy. 
Preliminary work suggests, for example, that the threshold for electrically- 
induced maximal seizures (criterion: tonic extension of the hind-limbs), ex- 
amined at 3 to 4 months of age, is lower in such brain-injured animals than in 
sham-treated controls. As might be expected, the incidence of sound-induced 
seizures, studied at 15 to 19 months, is not altered by the electroshocklesions. 
Most interesting would be a determination of the functional activity and con- 
nections of the nerve fibers newly populating the originally injured area. Some 
electrophysiologic work related to this question has been done in the rat (Kruger 
& Clemente, 1964) and cat (Malis, 1964) with laminar cortical lesions, similar to 
ours, produced by heavy ionized particles from a linear accelerator or cyclotron 
beam. The special characteristics of the electroshock (and the heavy particle- 
produced) lesions, for example, the absence of significant vascular disturbance 
and of glial scarring, and the repopulation of the injured area by axons which

title: Neurological evaluation of children with learning disorders
abstract_extracted: Neurological findings in 40 children referred with the principal of complaint of school learning problems are reviewed. Speech disorders and hyperkinetic syndromes were the most common features of the anamnesis. The final diagnosis in these subject's were: Minimal Brain Dysfunction (23), Behavior Disorder of Childhood (11), Mental Retardation (4), Acute Infantile Hemiplagia (1), High Myopia (1). Seizures disorders and borderline cerebral palsy syndromes are the most important neurological conditions to be excluded. It is believed that the distinction between minimal brain dysfunction syndromes and behavior disorders of childhood cannot be reliably based upon soft neurological signs, borderline EEG abnormalities or evidence of perceptual disturbances on psychological testing.

logical evaluation with the principal
complaint of school learning difficul-
ties is occurring with increasing fre-
quency in pediatric neurology facilities.
These children are sent to a neurologist

ptoms with multiple determinants and

The low incidence of overt neuro- 
logical abnormalities in children with 
learning disorders specifically refer- 
red for neurological consultation is 
strikingly evident. This will come as 
no surprise to those familiar with the 
characteristics of children with learning 
problems. Referral to a neurologist is 
usually motivated more by confusion 
and anxiety regarding an underachiev- 
ing child than by concern over a neuro- 
logical symptom. 
It is to be emphasized that this an- 
alysis refers to childen referred with 
the principal complaint of school le- 
arning problems. It is well known that

The detection of this type of EEG pat- 
tern indicates the need for a careful 
analysis of the child's behavior focus- 
sing on a search for seizure phenomena 
such as brief alterations of conscious- 
ness, lipsmacking, chewing movements, 
disorientations or other behavioral 
automatisms (GOLDENSOHN, 
E. S., and 
GOLD, A. P., 1960; GLASER, G. H., 
and DIXON, M. S., 1956). However, 
clinical evidence of seizure states are 
rarely found in these children, even 
those with paroxysmal EEG distur- 
bances. The significance of EEG find- 
ings of this type in children with learn- 
ing disorders is yet to be determined 
but may well adversely affect cogni- 
tive functions. 
Having excluded major neurological 
syndroms, the pediatric neurologist is 
faced with the task of formulating a 
diagnosis and set of recommendations 
for the bulk of children who do not fit 
into well-defined syndromes. The re- 
cognition of borderline mental retarda- 
tion, regardless of etiology, is impor- 
tant because of its educational and 
social implications. Ten percent of the 
present series fell into the category of 
mental retardation. Reliance on ab- 
breviated office testing for diagnostic 
appraisal is often quite deceptive. The 
developmental history may give a bet- 
ter index as to overall mental func- 
tions, but must be supplemented by 
formal psychometric testing whenever 
a question of mental retardation arises. 
The WISC or Stanford Binet are 
usually adequate for this purpose. 
The most difficult aspect of an eva- 
luation consists of distinguishing be- 
tween minimal brain dysfunction syn- 
dromes and behavior disorders of 
childhood. This corresponds to the 
categories of primary reading retarda- 
tion (developmental dyslexia) and se- 
condary reading retardation 
(exo- 
genous factors such as anxiety or poor 
schooling) developed by RABINOWITCH 
and coworkers (RABINOWITCH, 
R. D., 
et al., 1954). "Soft" neurological signs 
such as clumsiness, choreiform move- 
ments, dysdiadochokinesis, mixed late- 
rality, synkinesias, motor impersistence 
and others have been regarded as evi- 
dence of subtle disturbances of brain 
function by many authors (SCHAIN, 
R. J., 1968). This concept was first 
advanced by BENDER in her studies of 
severely disturbed children diagnosed 
as childhood schizophrenia (BENDER, 
L., 1947). Borderline EEG abnormali- 
ties are often used to reinforce this 
concept. From the psychometric side, 
scatter in subtest scores of the WISC 
or Stanford Binet and evidence of spa- 
tial confusions in the B E N D E R G ~ s ~ ~ ~ ~
or 
Goodenough Draw A Person test have 
been interpreted to indicate cerebral 
damage. However, careful analysis of 
the use of most of these approaches re- 
veal that they cannot be relied upon 
to distinguish poor performance due to 
adverse environmental factors and 
cerebral dysfunction of endogenous 
origin (SCHULMAN, 
J. E., et al., 1965; 
HERBERT, 
M., 1964; PAINE, R. S., et 
al., 1968). Normative data for most of 
the soft neurological signs is lacking. 
The standard intelligence tests such as 
the WISC or Stanford Binet were 
originally developed for the measure-

the presence or absence of serious be-

All studies of children with behavior 
disorders indicate a male preponder- 
ance of 3 to 4 : 1 or higher (BAHN, A. 
et al., 1961; BENTZEN, F., 1963). In 
this study, in which an effort was made 
to separate psychogenic behavior pro-

the incidence was only 1.6 : 1 in favor 
of males in the latter group as compar- 
ed to 4.5 :I in the presumed psycho- 
genic group. HALLGREN'S 
(HALLGREN, 
B., 1950) monumental study in this 
area reported investigations on 112 
cases of "specific dyslexia" and 160 
secondary cases (sibs and parents of 
probands). This is virtually the only 
report in which test procedures were 
administered to entire families. The in- 
cidence of dyslexia in males, as usual, 
was higher than in females in primary 
cases but was almost equally distribut- 
ed among the sexes in the secondary 
cases. HALLGREN 
concluded that fac- 
tors extraneous to genetically deter- 
mined learning difficulties may explain 
the male preponderance. It may be 
that behavioral reactions to the frus- 
trations produced by learning diffi- 
culties are the sex-linked aspect of the 
problem.

The management of children with 
learning disorders is a function of the 
final diagnostic formulation. This re- 
quires co-operation with a variety of 
other professionals, especially in the 
area of special education and family 
counselling. Neurological aspects of 
therapy will primarily be concerned 
with the use of drugs in the control of 
hyperkinesis and improvement of at- 
tention span. Barbiturates should not 
be used as paradoxical reactions in the 
form of excessive irritability and in- 
creased activity frequently occur. Dex- 
troemphetamine (5-30 mgm./day) and 
Methylphenidate (10-80

1966 5

should be administered in the same

response or an adverse reaction occurs.

syndrome may lie in its use prior to the 
time when a learning disorder has be-

present, a trial of primadone or di- 
phenylhydantoin may be warranted.

reinforced by a wish to avoid recogni-

title: Brain function in problem children and controls: psychometric, neurological, and electroencephalographic comparisons
abstract_extracted: Psychometric. neurological, and EEG studies were made of 24 children with scho- lastic-behavioral problems but no classical evidence of neurological disease and of 24 matched controls. Differences between the two groups were significant in all three measures, giving evidence of brain dysfunc- tion in the groups with scholastic-behavior- al problems. Two subgroups-hyperactive and nonhyperactive-each with character- istics suggesting a different syndrome, are described.
